public_rationale: All three named industries had established safety-evaluation requirements. FDA requires drug companies to test products and submit safety-and-effectiveness evidence. FAA requires applicants to demonstrate compliance with airworthiness standards. Vehicle manufacturers certify compliance with federal safety standards using a reasonable evidentiary basis. These systems differ, but they support Marcus's limited observation that evaluating products against safety requirements is common outside AI.
limitations: The evidence establishes the three named U.S. examples, not a numerical survey of every industry or jurisdiction.
Automobile certification does not require manufacturers to reproduce every government test procedure.
The existence of these systems does not establish that SB-1047's particular requirements were effective or proportionate.
Outcome dates represent standing regulatory practices at publication; the cited documents were issued earlier.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Asking for standards is not unique to AI: in many industries, such as pharmaceuticals, aviation and automobiles, it is common to ask companies to evaluate the safety of their products against set standards.

statement.excerpt: Lastly, asking for standards is not unique to AI; it's common across many industries to ask that companies evaluate the safety of their products according to set standards: just look at the pharmaceutical industry, or aviation, automobiles, etc.
statement.document_title: An open letter to Fei-Fei Li concerning California’s proposed AI regulation, SB-1047

our_interpretation: Read this as an observation that established safety-evaluation requirements exist across the three named industries.
Use United States regulatory practice, consistent with the California policy discussion and the named examples.
Safety evaluation includes testing, documented analysis and demonstrating compliance. It does not require identical approval procedures across industries.

Because this describes an ongoing institutional practice, assess the regulatory state as of August 10, 2024. Earlier official documents establish standing requirements; their publication dates are recorded separately from the date those requirements held.
criteria.support_condition: Official records establish routine product-safety evaluation against defined requirements in pharmaceuticals, aviation and automobiles by the post date.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Reliable regulatory records show that safety evaluation against defined requirements was generally absent in the named industries, making the asserted cross-industry practice materially inaccurate.

evidence.excerpt: Drug companies seeking to sell a drug in the United States must first test it. The company then sends CDER the evidence from these tests to prove the drug is safe and effective for its intended use.
evidence.locator: Developing New Drugs, paragraph beginning 'Drug companies seeking'
evidence.explanation: FDA describes manufacturers testing drugs and submitting evidence against a defined safety-and-effectiveness requirement. The event date denotes this standing regulatory practice at the post date, not the document's publication.

evidence.excerpt:
The
certification basis identifies the specific 14 CFR parts and amendment levels with which the
applicant must show compliance before the issuance of the TC. The certification basis includes
the applicable airworthiness standards for the category of the TC to be issued.
evidence.explanation: The FAA order requires applicants to demonstrate compliance with specified airworthiness standards before type certification. This documents the standing aviation certification framework at the post date.

evidence.excerpt:
A manufacturer may base its certification on, for example, simulations or

engineering analyses if it exercised reasonable care in certifying that the vehicle would meet the

standard when tested by NHTSA using the standard’s test conditions and procedures.
evidence.locator: Section I, Introduction, paragraph discussing methods of manufacturer certification
evidence.explanation: NHTSA explains how manufacturers evaluate vehicles against federal safety standards when certifying compliance. It also limits the analogy: manufacturers may use simulations or analysis instead of reproducing NHTSA's exact tests.
